newsitem.title: USA: U.S. largest silver user but demand sluggish--GFMS.
newsitem.headline: U.S. largest silver user but demand sluggish--GFMS.

text.p: Demand for silver in the U.S. rose only two percent in 1996 and fell marginally in Europe and Japan, leaving the rise in Indian demand to boost aggregate world silver demand last year, Gold Field Mineral Services Ltd (GFMS) said in its 1997 "World Silver Survey" published Wednesday on behalf of Silver Institute.

"While the U.S. remained the largest user of silver last year, on account of its leading position in industrial, photographic and coin fabrication, India became the second largest fabricator, ahead of Japan," one of the report's authors, Philip Klapwijk, told analysts in New York.

"By far, the largest contribution to the increase in world demand came from India, where jewelry and silverware continue to dominate the demand picture," Klapwijk said. "The falling price of silver during the year led to a price-elastic response in the form of higher demand in India."
Silver demand is composed of four main categories -- jewelry and silverware, photography, industrial applications, and coin fabrication.
Jewelry and silverware demand worldwide rose 17 percent in 1996 to 263 million ounces (8,180 tonnes), with more than half of the world's fabrication accounted for by India and Italy.
Jewelry and silverware fabrication in North America registered another double-digit increase to a record 28 million ounces (870 tonnes).
But nearly all the growth came from Mexico, with US fabrication declining slightly for the first time since 1991, according to the GFMS report.
The amount of silver used in photographic products rose 1.4 percent last year worldwide to 226 million ounces (7,030 tonnes).
North America remains the largest regional user of silver for photographic purposes, consuming 78.6 million ounces last year against worldwide photography consumption of 226.2 million ounces.

"In terms of demand for color films last year, there was a marginal increase in Europe, with a somewhat stronger rise in North America, but the growth in color film was driven principally by higher sales to developing country markets," GFMS stated.

The most important development last year in consumer photography was the launch in April of the Advanced Photo System (APS), a new film format known as IX240, but APS uses about one-third less silver than standard 35mm film.
In professional photography, digital imaging will also continue to encroach on the traditional silver halide market, the report said.
Total silver use in coin fabrication fell 17 percent in 1996 to 20.8 million ounces (647 tonnes), led by a sharp fall in U.S. minting.

"With little change in either Mexico or Canada in 1996, coin fabrication demand was dominated by developments in the U.S., where production fell by almost 25 percent after four years when annual output had been maintained at just over eight million ounces (250 tonnes)," the report stated.

"Last year's total offtake of 6.1 million ounces (190 tonnes) was the lowest recorded since 1985, but U.S. remained easily the world's largest producer of silver coins, its output nearly double that of Germany, the second placed country," the report added. ((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
